key_terms.meaning: A converter system that holds a battery on a DC bus between a charger and an inverter so the load keeps running when the mains fails.
Rectifier charges the DC bus and the inverter always feeds the load, so the load never sees a mains dip; efficiency is lower than offline types.
Back-to-back thyristor pair that moves the load between the mains and the inverter in a few milliseconds, with no moving parts.
t = (V<sub>bat</sub> × Ah × DoD) ÷ P<sub>dc</sub>, where P<sub>dc</sub> = load watts ÷ inverter efficiency; the time a battery holds the load down to its allowed depth of discharge.
The charger holds a constant current until the battery reaches its voltage limit (14.4 V for a 12 V lead-acid block), then holds that voltage while the current tapers; both stages put charge in.
Delaying the TRIAC/SCR turn-on in each half cycle of the AC wave to set the RMS voltage fed to a lamp or heater.
Ah put in ÷ Ah taken out = 1 ÷ charge efficiency; about 1.11 for lead-acid at 90 %.
Copper coil carrying the high-frequency current that induces the heating current inside the metal workpiece placed near it.
δ = √(ρ ÷ (π f μ)), depth below the surface where current density falls to 1/e; higher frequency f gives a thinner hot layer.
Power dissipated as heat by circulating currents induced in the body of the workpiece, the main heating mechanism above the Curie temperature.
Inverter with a capacitor in series with the work coil, driven near resonance so the coil current is large and the switching loss is small.
End station of an HVDC link holding the converter transformers, valve hall and filters that turn AC into DC or DC back into AC.

key_terms.term: Firing angle α and extinction angle γ
key_terms.meaning: α sets when a valve starts conducting and γ is the margin left before the voltage reverses; γ must stay positive for successful commutation.
Capacitance current of an AC cable or long line that flows even at no load; it is absent on a DC line, which is why HVDC suits long cables.
Shunt device that varies its reactive output continuously by thyristor switching of reactors and capacitors, holding bus voltage nearly constant.
Fixed reactor in series with a thyristor pair; delaying the firing angle reduces the current and so the reactive absorption.
Voltage-source inverter connected through a reactor; it exchanges reactive current by making its output voltage larger or smaller than the bus voltage.
B<sub>L</sub>(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α] ÷ (π X<sub>L</sub>), from 1/X<sub>L</sub> at α = 90° to zero at α = 180°.
Power converter that synchronises its output current with the grid voltage and pushes power from a DC source into the AC network.
Current controller that switches when the actual current crosses a band of width ±h around the reference, giving fast, robust but variable-frequency operation.
Control that continuously adjusts the DC operating voltage so that a solar array delivers its maximum available power.
f<sub>s</sub> = (V<sub>dc</sub>² − v<sub>g</sub>²) ÷ (2 h L V<sub>dc</sub>) for a full bridge: highest at the grid zero crossing, lowest at the peak.
Set point is the wanted value of the controlled variable; error e = set point − measured value drives the controller output.
The final device that acts on the process, here a power converter or thyristor switch controlling heater or motor power.
Flow ∝ N, head ∝ N², power ∝ N³; at 80 % speed a pump takes about 51 % of full power.

takeaways: A UPS is a charger, a battery and an inverter on a shared DC bus; the topology chosen decides efficiency, transfer time and cost.
A battery charger is a controlled DC source following a fixed current-then-voltage profile, and the same thyristor switching runs dimmers, timers and emergency lamps.
Induction heating puts the heat source inside the workpiece, so it is fast, clean and controllable by frequency and coil current.
HVDC carries bulk power without line charging current, has no stability limit over distance and gives full, fast control of power flow.
Thyristor-switched reactors and capacitors in SVC and FACTS devices hold voltage and push a line closer to its thermal limit without building new lines.
A grid-tied converter with a fast current loop fixes power factor, limits harmonics and lets power flow in either direction between DC source and grid.
Hysteresis current control is popular for grid interfaces because it is simple and robust, at the cost of variable switching frequency and wider ripple.
Every process-control loop is sensor, transmitter, controller and actuator; the actuator here is a power converter whose duty or firing angle is set by the error.

Sizing rules matter in practice: battery Ah for backup time, charge time from the charge factor, PV Wp from daily energy and sun hours, SVC range from the TCR and capacitor, and HVDC pole current from P<sub>d</sub> = V<sub>d</sub> I<sub>d</sub>.
Level and pump loops use the same muscle as heater loops; a variable-frequency drive saves energy because pump power falls as the cube of speed.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine one block diagram with a worked number: draw the power circuit, mark the controlled switch and its firing or switching instants, explain how the output (voltage, current, temperature, level) is held, and finish with a sizing or rating calculation.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an on-line (double-conversion) UPS and explain the function of each block from mains input to load. Why does the load never see a mains failure?
outline: Input filter and rectifier/charger feeding the DC bus
Battery bank floating on the DC bus with cut-off and protection
Inverter (IGBT, sinusoidal PWM) and output filter giving a clean 50 Hz sine
Static bypass and maintenance bypass
Operation on mains, on failure and on bypass; why there is no transfer time
Numerical check of battery current and backup time
answer: Block diagram: mains → input filter and rectifier/charger → DC bus with the battery bank → inverter → output filter (and isolation transformer) → load. A static bypass switch joins the mains straight to the load, and a manual maintenance bypass runs round the whole UPS.

Input filter and rectifier/charger: the filter keeps the UPS's switching noise out of the mains and stops mains spikes. The rectifier (thyristor, or an IGBT active front end with near-unity power factor) turns the AC into DC, holds the DC bus voltage and supplies the inverter. The charger part keeps the battery at its float voltage and recharges it after an outage at a limited current.

Battery bank: lead-acid or lithium cells in series to the bus voltage (48 V in a small unit, a few hundred volts in a large one). It floats on the DC bus, so it is always connected and needs no switching. A low-voltage cut-off stops discharge at the allowed depth of discharge; a fuse or breaker protects the battery cables.

Inverter: a full-bridge (or three-phase) IGBT inverter with sinusoidal PWM makes a 50 Hz sine. An LC output filter removes the switching ripple, so output THD is low (below about 3 % for linear loads), and the control holds voltage and frequency steady even when the input is poor. It must supply the peak current of SMPS loads, whose crest factor is 2.5 to 3.

Static bypass: a thyristor switch that moves the load to the mains in a few milliseconds if the inverter is overloaded (for example by a motor starting) or develops a fault. The inverter stays synchronised to the mains so that this transfer does not jolt the load. Maintenance bypass: a manual switch path that isolates the whole UPS so it can be serviced while the load stays on the mains.

Operation on mains: mains → rectifier → DC bus → inverter → load, with the charger topping up the battery. On mains failure: the rectifier stops, and the battery, already on the bus, feeds the inverter. The inverter never stops and its output never switches path, so the load sees no break: the transfer time is zero. On mains return: the rectifier takes over the bus again and recharges the battery.

answer.text: Numerical check, with the UPS of the worked example (640 W at 0.8 power factor, η = 0.9, 48 V, 100 Ah, 80 % depth of discharge):

answer: Why it is chosen: the load is isolated from mains spikes, sags and frequency drift all the time, not only during an outage. The price is two conversions in series, so efficiency is a few per cent lower than an off-line unit, and the rectifier and inverter must both be rated for the full load.
Check: 14.8 A for 5.40 h is 80 Ah, which is exactly 80 % of the 100 Ah battery, so the backup time and the depth of discharge agree.

bank.q: Explain the constant-current then constant-voltage charging profile of a 12 V lead-acid battery and describe a regulated charger that produces it. Work out the charge time for a 100 Ah battery at 50 % depth of discharge.
outline: Why the current must be limited first; voltage limit and gassing
CC stage: current held, voltage rises
CV stage: voltage held, current tapers; float afterwards
Charger circuit: rectifier, regulator (series pass, buck or thyristor bridge), current and voltage sensing, lower-demand-wins logic
Charge factor and time worked out
answer: Why a profile: a discharged battery has a low terminal voltage, so a fixed-voltage source would push a very large current, overheat the cells and the charger. Near full charge, a voltage above about 2.4 V per cell (14.4 V per 12 V block) makes the cells gas and lose water. So the charger first limits the current, then limits the voltage.
CC stage: the charger holds the current at a set value, often 0.1C (10 A for 100 Ah). The terminal voltage rises steadily as the charge goes back in. This stage returns most of the charge.

CV stage: when the voltage reaches 14.4 V, the charger holds it there. The battery's internal voltage keeps rising, so the current falls (tapers). Charging ends when the current falls to a set value, for example 2 A, or on a timer; then the charger drops to a float voltage of about 13.5 to 13.8 V that only makes up self-discharge.

Charger circuit: a transformer and diode bridge (or a thyristor bridge) with a capacitor filter make raw DC. A regulator sits between this DC and the battery: a series pass transistor, a buck converter, or the phase-controlled thyristor bridge itself. A milliohm current-sense resistor gives V<sub>s</sub> = I R<sub>s</sub>; a divider gives the battery voltage. Two error amplifiers compare these with their references, and the one that asks for less output controls the regulator (the "lower demand wins"), so the charger is in CC until the voltage limit and in CV after it. Temperature sensing lowers the voltage limit when the battery is hot; protection covers reverse polarity, over-current and over-temperature.

answer: A common mistake is to say that the CC stage returns all 55.6 Ah (5.56 h) and then add a taper on top. The CV stage also puts charge in, so the CC stage ends earlier.
Check: 44.44 + 11.11 = 55.55 Ah, which is 50 Ah ÷ 0.90, so the two stages together return exactly the charge needed.

bank.q: Explain the principle of induction heating. Why is the heat produced inside the workpiece rather than in the coil, and how is the frequency chosen?
outline: Alternating current in the work coil sets up an alternating field
Eddy currents and hysteresis heat the workpiece
Transformer model: coil primary, workpiece a shorted one-turn secondary, reflected resistance
Skin depth formula and the choice of frequency, with the Curie point
Resonant inverter and capacitor for the low power factor
answer: Principle: a high-frequency current in a copper work coil sets up an alternating magnetic field. A metal workpiece inside the coil links this field, so by Faraday's law an EMF is induced in it. The EMF drives eddy currents round the workpiece, and the workpiece's own resistance turns them into I²R heat. In magnetic steel below the Curie point, hysteresis loss adds a little more heat each cycle.

Transformer model: the coil is the primary of N turns; the workpiece is a single shorted turn as the secondary. Seen from the coil, the workpiece appears as a reflected resistance R<sub>ref</sub>, so the power into the metal is P ≈ I<sub>coil</sub>² R<sub>ref</sub>. The large magnetising inductance makes the coil current lag, so the power factor is low, often 0.1 to 0.3.

Why the heat is in the workpiece: the coil is thick copper of low resistance and is water-cooled, so its I²R loss is small and is carried away. The workpiece has higher resistivity and the eddy current is crowded into a thin surface layer, so its effective resistance is much higher. The same current therefore makes most of its heat in the metal.

Skin depth: δ = √(ρ / (π f μ)). The current density falls to 1/e of its surface value at depth δ. Higher frequency gives a thinner heated layer: surface hardening uses high frequency, through-heating of a billet uses low frequency. A rule of thumb is δ of about one-third to one-half of the billet radius for through-heating.

answer.text: Numbers for steel (ρ = 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m and μ<sub>r</sub> = 100 cold; ρ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m and μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 hot, above about 770 °C):

answer: Choosing f: the hot stage is the hard one, because above the Curie point δ grows about 25 times. For the 50 mm billet of the worked example, δ = 12.5 mm (half the radius) needs f = ρ / (π μ<sub>0</sub> δ²) = 1945 Hz, so a 2 kHz supply is used.

Supply: a resonant inverter (series or parallel) with a tank capacitor drives the coil near resonance. The capacitor supplies the coil's vars, so the inverter carries only the real power: in the worked example 18.8 kW at 400 V, 47 A instead of 157 A.
Check: at 2 kHz, δ = √(1.2 × 10⁻⁶ / (π × 2000 × 4π × 10⁻⁷)) = 12.3 mm, close to the 12.5 mm aimed at.

bank.q: Explain HVDC transmission with a two-terminal block diagram and list its advantages over EHV AC transmission. Find the pole current of a ±500 kV, 2000 MW bipolar link.
outline: Converter stations at both ends: converter transformers, 12-pulse valves, smoothing reactors, AC and DC filters, earth electrode
Rectifier and inverter operation; line commutation and reactive power
Monopolar and bipolar links
Advantages: no charging current, cables, asynchronous links, fast power control, two conductors
Pole current and pole-out power
answer: Block diagram: AC system A → converter transformer → 12-pulse thyristor converter (rectifier) → smoothing reactor → DC line → smoothing reactor → 12-pulse converter (inverter) → converter transformer → AC system B. AC filters and capacitor banks sit on both AC buses; DC filters and an earth electrode sit on the DC side.

Converter transformer: a star-star and a star-delta winding feed two six-pulse bridges 30° apart, which together make a 12-pulse converter. It also insulates the AC side from the DC voltage and sets the AC voltage by its taps.

Valves: thyristors in series. At the sending end the firing angle α is below 90° and the bridge rectifies; at the receiving end it is above 90° and the bridge works as a line-commutated inverter, with an extinction angle γ kept for safe turn-off.

Smoothing reactor: keeps the DC current continuous at light load and limits the rise of current in a DC fault. AC filters: tuned to the 11th and 13th harmonics (the lowest left by a 12-pulse bridge), plus a high-pass branch; they also supply part of the reactive power, which each station absorbs at about half its DC power.
Monopolar: one conductor and earth or metallic return. Bipolar: a +pole and a −pole; in balance the earth current is nearly zero, and if one pole trips the other carries on with earth return.

Advantages over EHV AC: (1) no charging current, so long cables and long overhead lines carry only useful current; (2) no stability limit from the angle between the ends, so length is limited only by losses; (3) two systems of different frequency or not in step can be joined; (4) power is set fast and exactly by converter control and can be reversed; (5) two conductors instead of three and smaller towers, so beyond the break-even distance (hundreds of km overhead, a few tens of km in cable) DC is cheaper; (6) a DC link does not add to the fault level of the AC systems.
Disadvantages: costly converter stations, harmonics and filters, reactive power demand, and DC breakers that are hard to build.

answer.text: Pole current of the ±500 kV, 2000 MW bipolar link:
answer.pre:
V<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 500 kV = 1000 kV (pole to pole)
I<sub>d</sub> = P<sub>d</sub> / V<sub>d</sub> = 2000 × 10⁶ / (1000 × 10³) = 2000 A in each pole
One pole out: P = 500 kV × 2000 A = 1000 MW
Reactive power per station ≈ 0.5 × 2000 = 1000 MVAr

answer: Check: each pole carries 500 kV × 2000 A = 1000 MW, and two poles give the 2000 MW.

bank.q: A home needs 600 W of backup at 0.8 power factor for 4 hours from a 24 V battery bank. Allowing 85 % inverter efficiency, 80 % depth of discharge and a 25 % margin on the inverter rating, find the battery Ah, the battery current and the inverter VA rating. How long does a 15 A charger take to put the charge back at 90 % charge efficiency?
outline: Energy at the load = 2400 Wh
Battery energy = 2400 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 2824 Wh
Ah = 2824 ÷ 24 ≈ 117.6 Ah used; ÷ 0.8 gives 147 Ah, choose 150 Ah
Battery current 29.4 A
Inverter: 600 ÷ 0.8 = 750 VA, × 1.25 = 938 VA, choose 1 kVA
Recharge: 117.6 ÷ 0.9 = 130.7 Ah, at least 8.7 h at 15 A
answer: Given: P = 600 W, cos φ = 0.8, t = 4 h, V<sub>bat</sub> = 24 V, η<sub>inv</sub> = 0.85, DoD = 0.8, margin 25 %, charger 15 A, charge efficiency 0.90.
Energy the load needs: E<sub>load</sub> = P × t = 600 × 4 = 2400 Wh.
Energy the battery must give: the inverter loses 15 %, so E<sub>bat</sub> = 2400 / 0.85 = 2823.5 Wh.
Ah actually taken out: 2823.5 / 24 = 117.6 Ah.
Ah rating: only 80 % may be used, so C = 117.6 / 0.8 = 147.1 Ah. Choose a standard 150 Ah bank (two 12 V, 150 Ah batteries in series).
Battery current: P<sub>dc</sub> = 600 / 0.85 = 705.9 W, so I = 705.9 / 24 = 29.4 A. Check: 29.4 A × 4 h = 117.6 Ah, as above.

Inverter rating: S = P / cos φ = 600 / 0.8 = 750 VA. With a 25 % margin for starting surges (a fridge or fan motor), 750 × 1.25 = 937.5 VA, so choose a 1 kVA inverter. It must be rated in VA, not watts, because current heats the switches.

Rate check: a 4-hour discharge is faster than the 20-hour rate printed on a lead-acid block, so the block gives somewhat fewer Ah. Check the 150 Ah choice against the maker's 4-hour rating and move up one size if that rating falls below 147 Ah.
Recharge: the charge taken out is 117.6 Ah; at 90 % efficiency the charger must put in 117.6 / 0.90 = 130.7 Ah.
At 15 A this takes at least 130.7 / 15 = 8.7 h. In practice the CV taper at the end makes it longer, roughly 10 h, so an overnight recharge is just enough.

head: Quantity
Value
rows: 24 V, 150 Ah (147 Ah needed at the 4-hour rate)

answer: Check: usable energy of the chosen bank = 24 × 150 × 0.8 = 2880 Wh, which is more than the 2823.5 Wh needed.

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 100 W incandescent lamp through a TRIAC with phase-angle control. Explain the DIAC-TRIAC firing circuit and find the lamp voltage and power at firing angles of 60° and 135°.
outline: RC network charges each half cycle; DIAC breaks over and fires the TRIAC
Conduction from α to the end of each half cycle
V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √(1 − α/π + sin 2α / (2π))
Numbers at 60° and 135°
Snubber, dV/dt, radio-interference filter
answer: Circuit: the TRIAC is in series with the lamp across the mains. A potentiometer R and capacitor C are connected across the TRIAC; the capacitor voltage lags the supply. A DIAC joins the capacitor to the TRIAC gate.

Firing: in each half cycle C charges through R. When its voltage reaches the DIAC breakover voltage (about 30 V), the DIAC conducts and dumps a current pulse into the gate, and the TRIAC turns on. It stays on until the current falls to zero at the end of the half cycle. The same happens in the negative half cycle, because both the DIAC and the TRIAC are bidirectional. Raising R slows the charging, so α increases and the lamp dims.

Waveform: the lamp sees the sine from α to π in each half cycle and zero before α. For a resistive load the RMS voltage is V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √(1 − α/π + sin 2α / (2π)), with α in radians.
Lamp resistance (treated as fixed): R = 230² / 100 = 529 Ω.
Conduction angle: the TRIAC conducts for π − α in each half cycle, 120° at α = 60° and only 45° at α = 135°.
Power falls much faster than α rises because P goes as V<sub>rms</sub>²: at α = 135° the lamp gets 30 % of the voltage but only 9 % of the power.

Supply current: the current jumps from zero to its full value at α, so it carries odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, …) and its fundamental lags the voltage. The supply sees a power factor below 1 even though the lamp is a resistor; the worst distortion is near α = 90°.

Practical points: an RC snubber across the TRIAC limits dV/dt so it does not fire falsely; an LC radio-interference filter is needed because the current jumps at α; a real filament is cooler and has lower resistance at low voltage, so it draws a little more power than these figures.
Check: at α = 90° the bracket is exactly 0.5, giving 162.6 V and 50 W, which lies between the 60° and 135° results as it must.

bank.q: Explain how an SVC built from a TCR and a fixed capacitor holds bus voltage. For a star-connected TCR of X<sub>L</sub> = 10 Ω per phase and a 60 MVAr fixed capacitor on a 33 kV bus, find the range of the SVC and the firing angle for zero output.
outline: Fixed capacitor gives leading vars, TCR gives lagging vars
B<sub>L</sub>(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α] / (π X<sub>L</sub>), from 1/X<sub>L</sub> at 90° to 0 at 180°
SVC output = Q<sub>C</sub> − Q<sub>L</sub>(α)
Voltage regulator measures bus voltage and sets α; V-I characteristic
Numbers: 108.9 MVAr, range −48.9 to +60 MVAr, zero at about 111°
answer: Circuit: on each phase a reactor L in series with two anti-parallel thyristors (the TCR), in parallel with a fixed capacitor bank (often built as harmonic filters). The SVC is a shunt susceptance B<sub>SVC</sub> = B<sub>C</sub> − B<sub>L</sub>(α).

TCR action: α is measured from the voltage zero crossing. At α = 90° the thyristors conduct fully and the reactor draws its full current; as α moves to 180° the conduction shrinks and the fundamental current falls to zero. The fundamental susceptance is B<sub>L</sub>(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α] / (π X<sub>L</sub>).

Voltage control: a controller measures the bus voltage. If the voltage falls, it raises α, the TCR draws less, the net output becomes more capacitive, and vars are supplied to lift the voltage. If the voltage rises, it lowers α and the SVC absorbs vars. Response takes one or two cycles. Inside its range the V-I characteristic is nearly flat with a small slope; at either limit it behaves as a fixed capacitor or reactor.

answer.text: Range of the given SVC (phase voltage 33 / √3 = 19.05 kV):

answer: Zero output: Q<sub>L</sub> must equal 60 MVAr, so B<sub>L</sub>(α) / B<sub>L</sub>(90°) = 60 / 108.9 = 0.551, that is [2(π − α) + sin 2α] / π = 0.551.
Capacitor size: 60 MVAr at 33 kV is B<sub>C</sub> = 60 × 10⁶ / (3 × 19,053²) = 0.0551 S per phase, so C = B<sub>C</sub> / ω = 0.0551 / 314.2 = 175 µF per phase in star.

Away from α = 90° the TCR current is not sinusoidal, so the TCR is built in delta (which traps the triplen harmonics) and the capacitor branches are tuned as 5th and 7th filters. The SVC also raises the transfer limit P = V<sub>S</sub> V<sub>R</sub> sin δ / X by holding V<sub>R</sub> up, and it can damp power swings by moving B quickly.
Check: at α = 111.1°, Q<sub>L</sub> = 108.9 × 0.551 = 60.0 MVAr, equal to the capacitor, so the net output is zero.

bank.q: Describe hysteresis current control for a single-phase grid-tied inverter. Explain the switching logic and band, derive how the switching frequency varies, and find it for V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V, L = 5 mH and h = 1 A on a 230 V grid.
outline: Reference current from grid phase and wanted power
Switch when the current leaves the band i<sub>ref</sub> ± h/2
Rise and fall times give f<sub>s</sub> = (V<sub>dc</sub>² − v<sub>g</sub>²) / (2 h L V<sub>dc</sub>)
Numbers: 40 kHz at the zero crossing, 13.6 kHz at the peak
Merits and faults; direction of power from the sign of the reference
answer: Reference: a phase-locked loop gives the grid angle ωt. The power controller sets the peak I<sub>m</sub> from the wanted power, so i<sub>ref</sub> = I<sub>m</sub> sin ωt. In phase with the grid voltage it exports power at unity power factor; in anti-phase it draws power (unity-power-factor rectification, for example charging a battery).

Logic: the measured inverter current i is compared with i<sub>ref</sub> + h/2 and i<sub>ref</sub> − h/2. If i rises above the upper edge, the bridge switches so that −V<sub>dc</sub> is across the leg and the inductor current falls. If i falls below the lower edge, it switches to +V<sub>dc</sub> and the current rises. The current therefore stays inside a band of width h round the sine.

answer.text: The current inside the band (drawn with a wide band so the switching can be seen):

svg.aria: A sine reference current with dashed upper and lower band edges and the actual current zigzagging between them, faster near the zero crossings.

answer: Switching frequency: while rising, the inductor voltage is V<sub>dc</sub> − v<sub>g</sub>, so the rise time is t<sub>1</sub> = h L / (V<sub>dc</sub> − v<sub>g</sub>). While falling it is V<sub>dc</sub> + v<sub>g</sub>, so t<sub>2</sub> = h L / (V<sub>dc</sub> + v<sub>g</sub>). One switching period T = t<sub>1</sub> + t<sub>2</sub> = h L · 2V<sub>dc</sub> / (V<sub>dc</sub>² − v<sub>g</sub>²), so f<sub>s</sub> = (V<sub>dc</sub>² − v<sub>g</sub>²) / (2 h L V<sub>dc</sub>).

answer.text: Numbers (V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V, L = 5 mH, h = 1 A, grid peak √2 × 230 = 325 V):

answer: So the frequency swings between 13.6 kHz and 40 kHz each half cycle. The output filter must be designed for the lowest frequency, 13.6 kHz; the switching loss is highest near the zero crossings where f<sub>s</sub> is highest.

Merits: very fast response (the current is corrected within one switching period), no carrier or PI tuning, the current error is bounded by h, it is robust to changes in L and the grid, and the same circuit charges or discharges a battery by changing the sign of i<sub>ref</sub>.

Faults: variable switching frequency spreads the harmonics over a wide band, which makes the filter harder and can cause audible noise; the losses vary through the cycle; and the frequency depends on L and V<sub>dc</sub>. Variants such as an adaptive band (h changed through the cycle) hold the frequency nearly constant.
Check: halving the band to 0.5 A doubles both frequencies to 80 kHz and 27.2 kHz, as f<sub>s</sub> ∝ 1/h says.

bank.q: Explain closed-loop temperature control of a furnace using a thyristor power controller, naming every element of the loop. A 2 kW, 230 V heater is used: find the firing angles for 50 % and 25 % power.
outline: Sensor (thermocouple or PT100) and 4–20 mA transmitter
Set point, error, PID controller
Actuator: anti-parallel thyristors, phase-angle or integral-cycle firing
Numbers: R = 26.45 Ω, α = 90° and 113.8°
Protection and isolation
answer: The loop: set point → summing point (error e = set point − measured temperature) → PID controller → thyristor power controller → heater → furnace → sensor and transmitter → back to the summing point.

Sensor and transmitter: a thermocouple (high temperatures) or a PT100 resistance thermometer measures the furnace temperature. The transmitter turns it into 4–20 mA, which survives long cables; 4 mA is the 0 % reading, so 0 mA shows a broken wire.

Controller: compares the measured value with the set point. Proportional action gives an output proportional to the error; integral action removes the steady error; derivative action damps overshoot. Its output is 0–100 %.

Actuator: two anti-parallel thyristors (or a TRIAC for small heaters) in series with the heater. In phase-angle firing the output sets α each half cycle; in integral-cycle (burst) firing it sets how many whole cycles out of a fixed period are on. Phase angle gives smooth control but harmonics and radio noise; burst firing switches at zero crossings and avoids them, but the heater gets bursts of full power.

answer.text: Firing angles for the 2 kW, 230 V heater (power fraction p = (V<sub>rms</sub> / V<sub>s</sub>)², and 1 − α/π + sin 2α / (2π) = p):

answer: Working: R = 230² / 2000 = 26.45 Ω. For 50 % the bracket must be 0.5, and at α = 90° it is 1 − 0.5 + 0 = 0.5. For 25 % it must be 0.25; α = 110° gives 0.287 and α = 115° gives 0.239, and solving between them gives α = 113.8° (1.987 rad), where the bracket is 0.250.

Ratings and protection: each thyristor carries an RMS current of 8.70 / √2 = 6.15 A and an average of 3.92 A; voltage rating 2 to 2.5 times the 325 V peak; fast fuse, RC snubber and heatsink. The gate circuit is isolated from the controller by an optocoupler or pulse transformer.
Check: at 25 %, P = 115² / 26.45 = 500 W, which is a quarter of 2 kW.

bank.q: Explain liquid level control of a tank using a power electronic actuator, and state what changes if the pump is fed by a variable-frequency drive. A pump takes 7.5 kW at full speed: find its power at 80 % and 60 % speed.
outline: On-off control with two probes or a float; hysteresis band; contactor or SSR
Continuous control: level transmitter, PID, VFD
Pump affinity laws Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³
Numbers: 3.84 kW and 1.62 kW
Dry-run protection, soft start
answer: On-off control: two probes (or a float switch) mark the low and high levels. When the water falls to the low probe, the controller starts the pump through a contactor or solid-state relay; when it reaches the high probe, the pump stops. The gap between the probes is the hysteresis band, which stops the pump from starting many times a minute.

Band sizing: in a tank of 2 m² floor area with probes 0.4 m apart, the band holds 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 m³. If the pump adds a net 20 m³/h (0.333 m³ per minute), one fill takes 0.8 / 0.333 = 2.4 min, so the pump starts at most a few times an hour if the draw-off is slow. A wider band means fewer starts but a bigger swing in level.

Continuous control: a level transmitter (pressure at the tank bottom or an ultrasonic sensor) sends 4–20 mA to a PID controller. The controller compares it with the set level and sets the speed reference of a variable-frequency drive. For example, a transmitter spanning 0–2 m that reads 12 mA shows (12 − 4) / 16 = 50 %, that is 1.0 m.

The VFD: a diode rectifier, a DC link and a PWM inverter that keeps V/f constant, so the motor flux stays fixed while the speed changes. The pump then delivers just the flow needed to hold the level, instead of running flat out and stopping.
Affinity laws of a centrifugal pump: flow Q ∝ N, head H ∝ N², power P ∝ N³.

Why the VFD saves energy: throttling a valve also cuts the flow, but the motor still runs at full speed against a higher head and takes close to full power. With speed control the power falls as the cube of speed.
Other gains of the VFD: soft start (no starting current of 6 to 8 times rated, no water hammer), dry-run protection from the drive's own current reading, and the PID loop can sit inside the drive.
Limit: the head falls as N², so the pump must keep enough speed to lift water to the tank; below that speed the flow stops even though the motor still turns.
Check: halving the speed gives 0.5³ = 12.5 % of full power, 0.94 kW, which lies below the 60 % value as it must.

bank.q: Compare off-line, line-interactive and on-line UPS topologies for transfer time, efficiency, output quality and cost, and recommend one for a small office and one for a hospital operating theatre.
outline: Off-line: load on mains, 4–10 ms transfer, cheapest, least protection
Line-interactive: tap-changing or buck-boost regulation, shorter transfer
On-line: double conversion, zero transfer time, best output, lowest efficiency
Load power factor and crest factor; VA sizing
Justified choice for both cases
answer: Off-line (standby): the load runs on the mains through a filter; the charger keeps the battery full and the inverter is off. On a failure, a transfer switch moves the load to the inverter in about 4 to 10 ms. It is cheap and efficient (the load sees the mains directly), but it does not correct sags, surges or frequency drift, and its inverter often makes a stepped wave.

Line-interactive: the load still runs on the mains, but a tap-changing transformer or buck-boost stage corrects the voltage, and the bidirectional inverter/charger is always connected and synchronised. Transfer on failure takes a few milliseconds, and many sags are handled without using the battery. It is the usual choice for small loads.

On-line (double conversion): rectifier → DC bus with the battery → inverter → load, all the time. On a failure only the source of the DC bus changes, so the transfer time is zero, and the output is a clean regulated sine whatever the input does. The cost is higher and the efficiency a few per cent lower, because the power goes through two converters.

Sizing applies to all three: choose the VA rating from the load VA, not watts. Eight office PCs of 150 W at 0.8 power factor need 8 × 150 / 0.8 = 1500 VA, so a 2 kVA unit gives margin. SMPS loads draw current with a crest factor of 2.5 to 3, so the inverter must supply peaks well above the sine-wave peak.
Small office: a line-interactive UPS of about 2 kVA. PCs and routers ride through a few milliseconds, the voltage correction handles the usual sags, and cost and running loss are low.

Operating theatre: an on-line UPS. Monitors, ventilators and surgical equipment must see no break and no disturbance at all; the zero transfer time, regulated output and static bypass with redundancy justify the cost and the extra loss.
Check: a 2 kVA unit at 0.8 power factor supplies 1600 W, above the office load of 1200 W.

bank.q: Explain why a diode-bridge rectifier with a capacitor filter draws distorted current, and describe how unity-power-factor rectification and an active harmonic filter correct it. Find the power factor for a current THD of 100 % and of 5 %.
outline: Capacitor charges only near the voltage peak: narrow current pulses, high THD
PF = displacement factor × distortion factor = cos φ₁ / √(1 + THD²)
Active front end: current reference in phase with the supply, hysteresis or PWM current control
Active harmonic filter injects the harmonic currents in antiphase
Numbers: 0.707 and 0.999
answer: Cause: the capacitor holds the DC voltage near the peak of the supply. The diodes conduct only when the supply voltage rises above the capacitor voltage, a short time around each peak. The current is a train of narrow, tall pulses rich in 3rd, 5th, 7th … harmonics, with a high crest factor.
Power factor: PF = P / S = (V I₁ cos φ₁) / (V I) = cos φ₁ × (I₁ / I), where I₁ is the fundamental current. With THD = I<sub>h</sub> / I₁, the distortion factor is I₁ / I = 1 / √(1 + THD²).

answer.text: Numbers, with the fundamental in phase (cos φ₁ = 1):

answer: So a typical diode-capacitor front end wastes almost 30 % of the supply current rating on harmonics, even though its fundamental is in phase.

Unity-power-factor rectification: replace the diode front end by an active front end: a boost PFC stage or an IGBT bridge with an inductor on the AC side. A phase-locked loop gives the supply angle; the DC-voltage controller sets the amplitude; the current reference is i<sub>ref</sub> = I<sub>m</sub> sin ωt in phase with the supply. A hysteresis or PWM current controller forces the line current to follow it, so the current is sinusoidal and in phase, and power flows from AC to DC. The same circuit with i<sub>ref</sub> reversed returns power to the supply.

Active harmonic filter: when the load cannot be changed (many existing drives), a shunt voltage-source converter is placed beside it. It measures the load current, extracts the harmonic part (load current minus its fundamental), and injects the same harmonic currents with opposite sign. The supply then provides only the fundamental. It follows load changes and cannot resonate with the network, unlike a tuned passive filter, and it can supply vars like a STATCOM at the same time.

Limits: the filter's converter must switch fast enough to track the highest harmonic to be cancelled, its DC bus must be above the supply peak, and its inductor must be small enough to let the current change quickly.
Check: raising THD from 5 % to 100 % lowers the PF from 0.999 to 0.707, the factor √2 that the formula predicts for equal harmonic and fundamental current.

bank.q: A utility must move 1500 MW over about 1000 km and also needs voltage support on a weak receiving bus. Evaluate the choice between a ±500 kV HVDC link and a 400 kV AC line with an SVC.
outline: HVDC: pole current, reactive demand at both ends, no distance stability limit, asynchronous, break-even distance
AC: power-angle limit with line reactance, several circuits or series compensation needed
SVC: voltage support, transfer limit
Losses, harmonics and filters, protection, cost
Justified recommendation
answer: HVDC option: a ±500 kV bipolar link has V<sub>d</sub> = 1000 kV, so I<sub>d</sub> = 1500 × 10⁶ / (1000 × 10³) = 1500 A per pole. One bipole on one tower line carries the whole 1500 MW; if a pole trips, 750 MW still flows with earth return.

HVDC reactive power: each line-commutated station absorbs about 0.5 × 1500 = 750 MVAr, supplied by filters and capacitor banks. At a weak receiving bus this is a real problem (risk of commutation failure), so either an SVC or STATCOM is added there, or a VSC link is chosen, which needs no vars and can itself support the voltage.

answer.text: AC option: take a typical 400 kV line reactance of about 0.33 Ω per km per circuit, so X ≈ 330 Ω for 1000 km.
answer.pre:
P<sub>max</sub> = V² / X = (400 × 10³)² / 330 = 485 MW per circuit
At a safe angle δ = 30°: P = 485 × sin 30° = 242 MW per circuit
Circuits needed for 1500 MW ≈ 1500 / 242 ≈ 6.2, so 6 to 7

answer: So the AC route needs six or seven circuits, or fewer circuits with series capacitors (TCSC) to cut X, plus intermediate substations and shunt reactors to control the charging current and the voltage rise at light load.

SVC role: an SVC at the weak bus holds V<sub>R</sub> up; since P = V<sub>S</sub> V<sub>R</sub> sin δ / X, a higher V<sub>R</sub> raises the transfer at the same angle and improves stability after faults. It fixes the voltage problem, but it does not remove the angle limit over 1000 km.

Evaluation: at 1000 km the distance is well beyond the overhead break-even distance of a few hundred km, and the AC line needs many circuits and heavy compensation. HVDC carries the bulk power on one corridor with lower losses and full control.

Recommendation: build the ±500 kV HVDC link (a VSC link if the receiving system is very weak; an LCC link with an SVC or STATCOM at the receiving bus otherwise), and use the SVC for the local voltage support. Keep AC only if many loads must be tapped along the route.
Check: 1500 A × 1000 kV = 1500 MW, and 6.2 circuits × 242 MW = 1500 MW, so both options are sized for the same power.

bank.q: Evaluate induction heating against resistance heating for a domestic cooking plate and for surface hardening of a steel gear tooth.
outline: Heat made inside the workpiece versus conducted in from a hot element
Efficiency, speed, control and safety on the cooktop; pan must be magnetic
Hardening needs a thin heated layer: skin depth sets frequency
Resonant inverter, power factor and cost
Conclusion for each application
answer: Basic difference: a resistance heater makes heat in its own element, which then reaches the work by conduction, convection or radiation. Induction makes the heat inside the work itself, through eddy currents (and hysteresis in magnetic steel), so there is no hot element in between.

Cooking plate, induction: the coil under the glass is fed at about 20 to 50 kHz by a resonant inverter. The pan base is the shorted secondary. For a magnetic steel pan at 25 kHz, δ = √(2 × 10⁻⁷ / (π × 25,000 × 100 × 4π × 10⁻⁷)) = 0.14 mm, so the heat is made right at the base. Heating is fast, the plate surface stays cooler, power responds at once to the control, and the stove stops heating when the pan is lifted.

Cooking plate, resistance: a coil or radiant element heats a plate that heats the pan. It is cheap, works with any pan (aluminium, clay, copper), and needs no electronics, but it is slower, wastes heat from the hot plate, and stays hot after switch-off.
Verdict for cooking: induction wins on speed, efficiency and safety, at a higher price and with the need for a magnetic pan; resistance is the low-cost choice that suits every vessel.

Gear hardening, induction: only a thin surface layer must be heated above the hardening temperature and quenched, leaving a tough core. The layer depth is set by the frequency. For a hardened depth of about 1.5 mm in hot steel (ρ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m, μ<sub>r</sub> = 1): f = ρ / (π μ<sub>0</sub> δ²) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ / (π × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × (1.5 × 10⁻³)²) = 135 kHz. A shaped coil heats one tooth or the whole gear in a few seconds, and the heating is repeatable for every part.

Gear hardening, resistance: a furnace heats the whole gear through, so the core also hardens (it becomes brittle) unless the gear is carburised first, and a slow furnace cycle causes scaling and distortion.
Supply points for induction: a resonant inverter at the right frequency, a capacitor to supply the coil's vars (the coil power factor is low), water cooling of the coil, and higher capital cost.

Conclusion: for the cooktop, induction is better if magnetic pans are used and the cost is accepted. For surface hardening, induction is clearly better, because only induction can heat a thin, controlled layer quickly; resistance heating suits through-heating, not case hardening.
Check: raising the frequency from 2 kHz to 135 kHz cuts δ in hot steel from 12.3 mm to 1.5 mm, a ratio of √(135 / 2) = 8.2, as δ ∝ 1/√f predicts.

glossary.def: Any power electronic circuit that changes the form of electric power: AC to DC, DC to AC, DC to DC or AC to AC.
A converter that turns DC into AC, usually by switching devices in a bridge and shaping the output with PWM.
A converter that turns AC into DC; diode rectifiers are uncontrolled, thyristor rectifiers have a controllable output.
Four-layer latching switch that conducts only after a gate pulse and turns off only when its current falls below the holding value.
Bidirectional thyristor that conducts in both half cycles, which makes it the standard switch in lamp dimmers and small AC controllers.
Bidirectional trigger diode that breaks over at a fixed voltage and is used to fire a TRIAC in a simple RC phase-shift circuit.
Insulated gate bipolar transistor; voltage-controlled switch combining MOS gate drive with low ON-state drop, widely used in inverters and drives.
Pulse-width modulation: switching on and off at a fixed frequency and varying the on-time to synthesise a wanted average voltage.
D = Ton ÷ T, the fraction of the switching period a device conducts; it sets the output of DC-DC converters and the fundamental of inverters.
PF = P ÷ S, the ratio of real power to apparent power; it falls when current is out of phase with voltage or rich in harmonics.
THD = √(Σ Vn²) ÷ V1 over n ≥ 2, the ratio of all harmonic content to the fundamental, in per cent.
Q = V I sin φ, the power that oscillates between source and reactive element, in var or kvar; it loads the line without doing real work.
Diode placed across an inductive load to carry the stored current when the main switch turns off, protecting the switch and improving output.
Small RC or RCD network across a switching device that limits dV/dt and absorbs turn-off energy.
The process of transferring current from one device or phase to another; in line-commutated converters the supply voltage itself forces turn-off.
Condition where a grid-connected inverter keeps feeding a local network after the grid has tripped; anti-islanding protection must detect and stop it.
Battery energy storage system: a battery bank with a bidirectional converter that can both charge from and discharge into the grid.
A shunt converter that senses the load current, extracts its harmonic content and injects an equal and opposite current to clean the supply.
Thyristor controlled series capacitor: a thyristor-controlled reactor in parallel with a series capacitor, giving a variable series reactance in the line.
Flexible AC transmission system: power electronic controllers, shunt or series, that make an AC network controllable and raise its usable capacity.
Circuit that converts a sensor output into a standard signal, such as 4–20 mA or 1–5 V, for the controller.
Control law with proportional, integral and derivative terms on the error; it holds the process variable at the set point despite disturbances.
Turning a thyristor on only at the instant the supply voltage crosses zero, used for heaters to avoid the harmonics of phase control.
The unwanted AC component left on a DC voltage or current after rectification, usually reduced by filters or higher switching frequency.
The temperature, about 770 °C for steel, above which a magnetic material loses its magnetism; μ<sub>r</sub> falls to about 1 and the skin depth grows.
The fraction of a battery's capacity taken out; a deeper discharge gives more energy per cycle but shortens battery life.
Charge or discharge current scaled to capacity: for a C Ah battery, nC means n × C amperes, so 0.1C is 10 A for 100 Ah.
Peak value ÷ RMS value of a current or voltage; 1.41 for a sine, much higher for the pulsed current of an SMPS.
